subtype: Being the subject of office talk [Receiver]
passage:
Team lead's note, follow-up with Dolma.
Since Dolma's promotion to senior analyst was announced, I've heard the pantry version: that she got it because she is "close to the director", plus questions about why she still isn't married. Alka told me Dolma overheard some of it on Tuesday.
Since then, Dolma copies me on every email, even two-line replies. She stayed till nine twice this week redoing slides that were already fine. At lunch she sits with a different group each day, as if checking who is on her side. In our meeting she said, "I just want them to see I earned it," and then apologised three times for taking my time.
What I did next: I told Dolma plainly that the promotion was based on her project results, and put that in writing. I asked her to stop copying me on routine mail. At Friday's team meeting I said that colleagues' personal lives are not team business.

qa.q: How many times did Dolma stay till nine this week?
qa.a: Twice this week.

qa.q: What does Dolma copying the lead on every email suggest?
qa.a: Dolma feels exposed and anxious, trying to prove she earned the role and to control how others see her.

qa.q: How could the lead's steps help Dolma stop spending energy on her image?
qa.a: A written reason for the promotion and a public line against personal talk take away what she was trying to defend, so she can just work.

qa.q: What would change for Dolma if the team stopped the speculation?
qa.a: She could stop redoing finished slides and testing lunch tables, and put that energy back into her actual job.

grounding: Shows an employee who finds colleagues speculating about her promotion and private life, feeling exposed and over-managing her image.

"Did you see Preeti's handover notes again? Half empty," Kunal said by the printer. "Everyone's talking about it."
"I saw," Darshan said. "I'm going to talk to her."
"To her? Just mention it to Ma'am in the review."
"That's talking about her. I'd rather talk to her."
Later, in the small meeting room: "Preeti, got five minutes? It's about the night-shift handovers."
Preeti's face tightened. "What about them?"
"Twice this week I came in and didn't know which client tickets were still open. I lost an hour each time. I wanted to tell you first, not anyone else. Is something going on?"
Preeti was quiet. Then: "My mother's been in and out of hospital. I've been leaving in a rush."
"I'm sorry. Could we do a two-minute voice note instead of written notes, just for this month?"
"Yes. Thank you for coming to me. I'd heard people were talking."

qa.q: How much time did Darshan lose each time?
qa.a: An hour each time.

qa.q: What does Preeti's face tightening suggest?
qa.a: Preeti felt wary and defensive, bracing for criticism, especially since she had heard people were talking.

qa.q: What made Darshan's conversation with Preeti work?
qa.a: Darshan spoke privately, described the effect plainly, asked what was going on and offered a small fix instead of blame.

qa.q: How might Kunal see Darshan's choice?
qa.a: Kunal probably finds it odd or awkward, since chatting about Preeti or telling the manager felt easier than facing her.

grounding: Shows an adult with a concern about a colleague speaking to her directly and privately instead of to others, which prevents talk behind her back.

At the sandpit behind the nursery in Valencia, Alejandro spread his arms across the castle. "Only me and Esther. Esther's my best friend. Lucas can't play."
Lucas, holding a red bucket, stopped. Esther looked from one boy to the other.
Señora Ruiz crouched beside them. "In our sandpit, everyone gets a turn. Alejandro, what job could Lucas have?"
Alejandro thought hard. "He can... do the moat?"
Lucas's face lit up. He tipped his bucket of water, the moat flooded, and all three shrieked with laughter.

qa.q: What was Lucas holding?
qa.a: A red bucket.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro spread his arms across the castle?
qa.a: Alejandro felt possessive and a bit worried about sharing Esther, so he tried to control who could play.

qa.q: How did Señora Ruiz handle it gently?
qa.a: She stated the rule simply and asked Alejandro to find Lucas a job, so he chose to include Lucas himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Lucas when he was told he couldn't play?
qa.a: Lucas felt hurt and stuck, standing still with his bucket, then happy once he got the moat job.

grounding: Shows a young child declaring who can and cannot play, and an adult gently teaching that everyone gets a turn.

Dear Diary,
Today Amandeep and I started the SECRET EAGLES club. Only four members: me, Amandeep, Rhea and Tanvi. Rules: 1. Password is "thunder". 2. We sit on the last bench at lunch. 3. No telling anyone what we talk about. Amandeep made badges from bottle caps.
When Simran asked to join, Amandeep said, "Sorry, full." It felt SO good hearing that. Like we were special.
Simran went and sat with the Class 4 kids. Her face looked funny, like she was trying not to cry.
It's still the best club. I just hope nobody ever makes a club without me.
Gurpreet

qa.q: What is the club's password?
qa.a: "thunder".

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when Amandeep said "Sorry, full"?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt thrilled and special, "SO good", being inside the club while someone else was kept out.

qa.q: What could the Eagles do so the club stays fun without hurting anyone?
qa.a: Let anyone who asks join, or take turns inviting new members, so the fun doesn't depend on shutting someone out.

qa.q: What was it like for Simran being turned away?
qa.a: Simran was hurt and embarrassed, trying not to cry as she went to sit with the younger kids.

grounding: Shows children forming a named club with rules, enjoying the thrill of being chosen that depends on someone else being left out.

At recess in the Oslo school yard, Ulla's group sat on top of the climbing frame, sharing one pair of earbuds and laughing at something on a phone.
Rania stood by the fence with her lunchbox, pretending to read. She had practised a joke last night, a good one about the maths teacher's striped socks. She took three steps toward the frame, then stopped. Ulla glanced over, then turned back to the others.
Something in Rania's chest squeezed. She walked back to the fence and said, a little too loudly, to nobody, "Climbing frames are for babies anyway."
Then she read the same page of her book four times.

qa.q: What were Ulla's group sharing?
qa.a: One pair of earbuds.

qa.q: What was Rania feeling when she said "Climbing frames are for babies anyway"?
qa.a: Rania felt hurt and left out, and said it loudly to pretend she didn't care.

qa.q: What small step could help Rania at recess?
qa.a: A teacher or one of the group could invite her up with a simple "Want to listen?", or she could try the joke with one friendly person first.

qa.q: How might Ulla have seen Rania's three steps?
qa.a: Ulla may not have noticed much at all; to her it was a passing glance, not the big moment it was for Rania.

grounding: Shows a child watching the popular group with longing and hurt, trying to approach and then pretending not to care.

passage:
I'm Lokesh, and I sit by the window, so I see everything at break.
A new girl, Farah, spent her whole first week standing by the water cooler. Nobody was mean. Nobody asked her either.
On Monday we were one short for kho-kho. Deepika walked to the cooler and said, "We need one more. Want to be on my side?" No big speech. Farah nodded so fast her plait bounced.
She got caught twice at first. Deepika just said, "Run zig-zag," and tagged her in again.
By Wednesday Farah was shouting "Kho!" louder than any of us. I don't know what Farah was thinking that first day at the cooler, but she hasn't stood there since.

qa.q: Where did Farah stand during her first week?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: How did Farah seem to feel when Deepika invited her?
qa.a: Farah seemed excited and relieved, nodding so fast her plait bounced.

qa.q: What made Deepika's invitation work so well?
qa.a: It was simple and ordinary, with no fuss, and Deepika kept encouraging her after she got caught.

qa.q: How might Deepika see what she did?
qa.a: Deepika probably saw it as nothing special, since the team just needed one more, without realising how much it changed Farah's week.

grounding: Shows a child inviting a lone new classmate into a game without fuss, and how that small act changes her school days.

"Zainab! Saved you a seat," Naveen called from their old corner of the canteen, two samosas on a plate.
Zainab slowed. At the middle table, Tanya was waving too. Tanya, whose posts got three hundred likes, who had tagged Zainab in a story for the first time last night.
"Actually, Tanya asked me to sit with them today," Zainab said.
"Oh." Naveen looked at the second samosa. "Tomorrow, then?"
"Yeah. Maybe."
At the middle table, Tanya said, "Wait, you used to sit with that quiz guy?"
"Not really," Zainab said quickly. "He just sat near me."
Everyone laughed. Zainab laughed too, and checked her reflection in her phone screen.
Across the canteen, Naveen was eating alone, the second samosa still on the plate. Zainab looked away first.

qa.q: What was on Naveen's plate?
qa.a: Two samosas.

qa.q: What does Zainab looking away first suggest?
qa.a: Zainab feels a private ache of guilt, knowing she dropped a loyal friend to gain standing with Tanya's table.

qa.q: What could Zainab do tomorrow to begin repairing things?
qa.a: Sit with Naveen, admit that saying "not really" was unfair, and stop treating friendships as rungs on a ladder.

qa.q: What is lunch like for Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen feels hurt and lonely, eating by himself with the samosa he saved still on the plate 😔

grounding: Shows a teenager judging standing by who tags and sits with her, dropping an old friend to climb and feeling a private ache about it.

passage:
Every Monday, Varun could tell who was in favour just by watching Pranav's bench in the Class 10 corridor of their Hyderabad school. This week it was Kabir: Pranav shared his earphones with him and laughed at every joke. Last week it had been Rishi. Now Rishi stood at the edge, laughing a beat too late.
Nobody argued with Pranav. When he called the new cricket captain "a nobody", three boys agreed within seconds, though one of them had voted for that captain.
Varun had been in favour once, in Class 8. He remembered waiting for Pranav's reply to every message.
On Thursday Pranav said, "Rishi's getting so annoying, na?" Rishi went pale. Everyone looked at their shoes. Varun heard himself say, "He's fine, Pranav," and then his heart was pounding.

qa.q: Who was in favour with Pranav this week?
qa.a: Kabir was in favour this week.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling after saying "He's fine, Pranav"?
qa.a: Varun's heart was pounding; he felt scared of losing his place, yet steadier for finally speaking.

qa.q: What could the boys do so Pranav's moods stop ruling the group?
qa.a: Back each other up like Varun did, and make plans or opinions without waiting for Pranav's approval.

qa.q: What is it like for Rishi now that he is out of favour?
qa.a: Rishi feels anxious and unsure, laughing a beat too late and going pale when Pranav turns on him.

grounding: Shows a peer watching a group leader decide who is in favour each week, keeping everyone anxious and obedient.

subtype: Hierarchies by college, city and money [Observer]
passage:
Sabina,
You asked what college in Delhi is really like. Honestly? It's school again, only quieter about it.
In school, rank was obvious: who had the new bat, who sat with whom. Here nobody says anything, but everyone knows. The ones from big city schools, with polished English and trips abroad, sit at the front canteen tables. The ones from smaller towns, like me, drift to the back. When Rohan says something half-baked in smooth English, people nod. When Manoj from Gorakhpur says something sharp in mixed Hindi and English, there's a pause first. Internships go through people's uncles.
Nobody is rude. That's what makes it hard to point at.
I'm doing fine, and Manoj is my closest friend here. I just notice it everywhere now, like a sorting machine running in the background.
Write back. Tell me it's different at yours.
Shankar

qa.q: Where do students from smaller towns tend to sit?
qa.a: They drift to the back canteen tables.

qa.q: How does Shankar seem to feel noticing the sorting?
qa.a: Shankar feels uneasy and a little frustrated, because the ranking is polite and quiet but always there.

qa.q: What could Shankar do to push back against the quiet sorting?
qa.a: Keep sharing tables and ideas across groups, and back up points like Manoj's in class so they get heard on merit.

qa.q: What might it be like for Manoj when a sharp point gets a pause first?
qa.a: Manoj may feel undervalued and self-conscious, judged by accent and background instead of the idea itself.

grounding: Shows a student noticing that college status quietly sorts people by city, English fluency, money and connections.
